procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 7, 1967 of the Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench in Criminal Revision Application No. 306 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant was convicted on three counts by the Judicial Magistrate. He appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge. He then filed a revision before the High Court. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order, 1964, but maintained the conviction for the other two charges, modifying the sentences to imprisonment already undergone and a fine of Rs. 1,000 on each of the two counts.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal limited to two points: (1) whether the confiscation of the foodgrains in the house of the appellant was legal.

directions: The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the seized stock of juar set aside.
The rest of the order of the High Court maintained.

issue.issue_text: whether the confiscation of the foodgrains in the house of the appellant was legal

facts: The appellant was convicted for contravening two orders: the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and the Buldana District Juar (Price Control) Order, 1965.
A lower court had ordered the juar (foodgrains) seized from the appellant's house to be confiscated.
The appellant's conviction for contravening a third order, the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) Order, had been set aside by the High Court.
law: The appellant argued that the two orders he was still convicted under did not contain any provision authorizing a court to forfeit the foodgrains themselves.
application: The Supreme Court examined the two relevant orders.
It found that the Maharashtra Jowar Order only allowed for the forfeiture of "packages, coverings or receptacles" in which the juar was found, not the juar itself.
It also found that the Buldana District Juar Order authorized the Collector to seize stocks but did not empower the court to order their forfeiture.
The counsel for the State was unable to point to any provision in these two orders that would permit the court to forfeit the juar.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the order of forfeiture was illegal because there was no legal provision in the specific orders under which the appellant was convicted that authorized the court to confiscate the foodgrains. Therefore, the Court set aside the confiscation order.

issue.issue_text: whether r. 141 (2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 is not ultra vires the Defence of India Act

facts: The appellant argued that Rule 141(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, was ultra vires (beyond the legal power of) the Defence of India Act.
The basis for this argument was that the rule established a rule of evidence that was contrary to the existing law found in Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act.
law: Section 3(1) of the Defence of India Act grants the Central Government very wide powers to make rules necessary for securing the defence of India, public safety, and maintaining essential supplies.

Section 43 of the Defence of India Act states that the provisions of the Act or any rules made under it shall have effect "notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act."
application: The Court first determined that Rule 141(2) was validly made under the broad powers conferred by Section 3(1) of the Act. It reasoned that providing a method for proving the publication of orders in judicial proceedings was essential to the overall scheme of the Defence of India Rules.
The Court then addressed the argument that the rule was inconsistent with the Indian Evidence Act. It held that this inconsistency did not matter because of Section 43.

Section 43 explicitly allows for rules made under the Defence of India Act to override other existing laws. Therefore, even though Rule 141(2) might be contrary to the Evidence Act, it remains valid and effective due to the overriding power granted by Section 43.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that Rule 141(2) was not ultra vires the Defence of India Act. The rule was found to be within the rule-making power granted by Section 3(1), and Section 43 ensured it would have legal effect despite any inconsistency with the Indian Evidence Act.

arguments.issue_text: whether the confiscation of the foodgrains in the house of the appellant was legal
appellant_arguments: The forfeiture of the juar was illegal because the two orders under which the conviction was maintained, the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and the Buldana District Juar (Price Control) Order, 1965, did not contain any provision authorizing the court to forfeit the foodgrains themselves.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the State) was unable to point to any provision in the two relevant orders that authorized the forfeiture of the juar.

arguments.issue_text: whether r. 141 (2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 is not ultra vires the Defence of India Act
appellant_arguments: Rule 141(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence that is contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act.
respondent_arguments: There is no precedent, either in England or India, where a rule similar to Rule 141(2) has been challenged and declared ultra vires.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A rule made under the Defence of India Act is valid if it falls within the powers conferred by the Act, and by virtue of Section 43 of the Act, it will have effect notwithstanding any inconsistency with other enactments. Furthermore, a court can only direct the forfeiture of property if the specific order that was contravened explicitly provides for such forfeiture.
obiter: The learned counsel has not been able to show us any case in which a rule like r. 141 (2) has been challenged, much less declared ultra vires, both in England and in India.
The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that while the appellant's conviction was valid, the forfeiture of the seized juar was illegal. The conviction was upheld because Rule 141(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, was deemed to be a valid exercise of the rule-making power under the Defence of India Act, with Section 43 of the Act overriding any inconsistency with other laws. However, the forfeiture order was set aside because the specific orders under which the appellant was convicted did not contain any provision authorizing the court to forfeit the foodgrains themselves, a necessary prerequisite for such an action.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a rule made under the Defence of India Act falls within the powers conferred by Section 3(1) of the Act.
Whether Section 43 of the Defence of India Act, which gives the Act and its rules overriding effect, applies to a rule that is inconsistent with another enactment.
Whether the specific orders contravened by the appellant contained a provision authorizing the forfeiture of property, as contemplated by the Defence of India Rules.
why_appellant_lost: Rule 141(2) is within the powers conferred by Section 3(1) of the Defence of India Act, which grants very wide powers.

The fact that Rule 141(2) may be contrary to an existing act, such as the Indian Evidence Act, does not invalidate it, because Section 43 of the Defence of India Act provides that the Act and its rules shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other enactment.
Rule 141(2) is essential to the scheme of the Defence of India Rules, as the Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders and for proof of such publication in judicial proceedings.
why_respondent_won: Rule 141(2) falls within the wide powers granted by Section 3(1) of the Defence of India Act.
Section 43 of the Defence of India Act explicitly allows for rules made under it to be inconsistent with existing legislation, giving them overriding effect.
The rule is considered essential for the practical application of the Defence of India Rules, as it provides a necessary mechanism for proving that orders have been published.
